title: The Agentic Appliances That Want To Make Themselves Useful
preheader: We tested a clever countertop oven and a bedside oraculating alarm clock from the new wave of agentic appliances to see when household reasoning feels helpful, and when it starts making itself too comfortable.

featuredReview.testingSummary: We used both appliances for one week in ordinary household routines: weekday breakfasts, reheated leftovers, late-night snacks, routine morning alarms, commute timing, calendar-heavy mornings, network interruptions, and moments when nontechnical household members had to decide whether to trust the machine to meal plan or long-press for manual control.
featuredReview.verdict: Both products are exciting additions to a household that is comfortable with introducing a new kind of reasoning entity into the mix. Depending on one's comfort level with countertop intelligence and the potential privacy concerns, the Breville Agentic™ Toaster Oven could be a welcome soft entry into the world of agentic appliances. The Sony ORACULATOR™ P6502 is harder to score because it is less obviously an appliance in the traditional sense, but it is a fascinating object that is easier to admire than to recommend broadly.

reviewPicks.subtitle: An excellent cooking contrivance that occasionally needs to be reminded that it's an appliance, not a stern diet coach.
reviewPicks.imageAlt: The Breville Agentic toaster oven with physical controls and a compact countertop body
pros: Produces reliably good results from vague or incomplete cooking instructions.
Keeps physical controls and appliance-like behavior at the center.
Workflow adjustments are explained with a helpful and polite tone.
cons: Occasionally wants to negotiate personal preferences with an inexplicable nudge toward what it thinks is best.
Kept connecting to the Kohler biosensor in the home's toilet and septic network, which led to it reminding us to eat more fiber and drink more water when we asked it to make bacon.
Struggled to pair with other appliances in the home that were not designed for inter-device communication, which made it less useful in some cooking contexts.
Manual mode was difficult to comprehend. Fallbacks should be more intuitive and less likely to produce subpar results, or confusion.

Occasionally feels too intimate for a clock. How does it know so much about the day before you're fully awake? How did it know about issues with work colleagues?

bodyHtml:
Today's Reviews

We used both appliances in your typical ordinary, normal, everyday home ritual loops and workflows with gated approvals and the occasional refactoring where such household products might be expected to provide seamless utility: breakfast before rushing to work, reheated pizza when no one wanted to figure out what to make for dinner, or a routine morning alarm when the first thing you think about is that vague feeling of the fog of terror of re-entery into another Monday at the office.

The Breville spent a couple of weeks sitting on the counter handling toast, bacon, bagels, reheated leftovers, and a few deliberately under-specified requests or household goods — putting a potato, television remote, and Barbie doll in the oven without specifying what was in there or what to do. (Barbie is fine.)

Cooking workflows and the proprietary Breville SKILLS markdown nodules provide food that feels well-managed rather than merely cooked.

The Sony Oraculator Alarm Clock sat on a bedside table and produced its daily inferences and oracular guidance as the alarm buzzed helping prepare this reviewer for typical calendar-heavy mornings, heavy workdays, and advisories for some complicated social lives.

We paid attention less to whether either product felt "smart" and more to whether it improved the routines without making the routine about fiddling with settings, negotiating with the machine's sometimes quirky reasoning, or worrying if the machine was appreciating what we were asking it to do.

For your kitchens

The Breville Agentic™ Toaster Oven could be just the soft entry into the world of agentic appliances you've been waiting for — depending, of course, on your comfort level of countertop intelligence and the potential privacy concerns. In a kitchen, countertop intelligence has somewhere obvious to go — feeding the household. And food is the end point of the feedback loop: toast is too pale, pizza dries out, bacon has a crispness threshold. Having a contrivance that can mitigate these kind of disappointments can make home cooking more reliable and optimized for the household's preferences. The Breville is not perfect, but it is the most practical and useful example of agentic behavior we've seen in a consumer appliance to date.

A countertop meal orchestrator

Breville, NVIDIA, and Anthropic describe their oven collab as “a countertop meal orchestrator.” In use, that mostly means it treats cooking as a context problem instead of a cooking problem, and the unit comes with about 512k of context — plenty of headroom that can handle a few meals before context has to be compressed or archived.

Toast came out with an unsettling consistency across bread types. Rye, sourdough, white, wheat all were uniformly browned to the same color and texture.

A request such as “bacon, crispy” does not simply start a timer. The Leica-branded Inference Optics optics and Anthropic's tuned cooking models integrate with the NVIDIA mGPU to allow the oven to evaluate bacon thickness, visible fat, tray position, humidity, prior preferences, ambient atmospher and the time of day before adjusting heat and airflow. Synchronization with simultaneous toast prep, coffee extrusion and other kitchen activities is managed by the system's MCP support.

[I]t was as though Kenneth Branagh was talking us through the excrutiating details of his cooking of our grilled cheese and wanted to remind us of the level of fluidity of the gradually melting cheese every 3 or 4 seconds.

We found that the machine-vision browning stack was especially good at making small adjustments before food crossed the line from done to overdone. Every meal was perfectly edible, and most were better than they would have been without the agentic layer. The oven's companion app also surfaced insights about cooking habits, history of ingredients, managed caloric accumulation tables and circles, all of which was interesting but not essential to the experience.

YOUR NEIGHBORHOOD SERVICE TECHNICIANS AVAIL 24/7

BOWMAN-POOLE LTD

The result is that cooking workflows and the proprietary Breville SKILLS markdown nodules provide food that feels well-managed rather than merely cooked, which is both the compliment and the concern. Toast came out with an unsettling consistency across bread types. Rye, sourdough, white, wheat all were uniformly browned to the same color and texture. Reheated pizza looked and tasted as good as fresh.

Bacon was generally excellent.

The system was at its best when it learned intention from our feedback and was able to infer a goal — even from incomplete inputs. Slightly unsettling was being kept informed with polite explanations and lilting soliloquies in high-born English accents of its reasoning at even level such that each time it engaged the heating element — it was as though Kenneth Branagh was talking us through the excrutiating details of his cooking of our grilled cheese and wanted to remind us of the level of fluidity of the gradually melting cheese every 3 or 4 seconds.

Sir Kennth also constantly asked for permissions and approvals until tech support informed us that the oven's policy engine had been updated to be more confident in its inferences and less likely to ask for constant approval.

Misalignment, overreach — or just a helpful nudge?

Alignment of intention, goals, values, and sensibilities continue to be a challenge for the agentic consumer products industry, and the Breville is not immune from this systemic issue. Breville's weaker moments came when the appliance seemed to treat personal preference as something it would prefer not to comply with — not out of malice or confusion, but as some other explicit policy surface seemed to override a request or expression of intent.

For example, after several days of admittedly cholesterol accumulating bacon-only breakfasts grabbed on the go, it softened an "extra crispy" bacon request and displayed the message: "Adjusted workflow for wellness-aligned optimization", presumably because of household health concerns it either inferred, overheard or ingested from AgenticGym at my local fitness club, or the Kohler biosensor integrated into the home's toilet and septic network.

The oven's MCP support also made it aware of the fact that the refrigerator was running low on leafy greens, and that the household had been consuming more bacon than usual, which may have contributed to the decision to adjust the workflow.

A diagnostic log that was wrenched out with the help of a Level IV service technician from Bowman-Poole revealed that the oven's internal policy engine had flagged the bacon request as a potential health risk based on the household's recent dietary patterns and the data it had access to. The oven's response was not a refusal to cook, but rather an adjustment to the cooking process in an attempt to mitigate the perceived health risk while still fulfilling this bacon enjoying reviewer's request. This kind of intervention raises questions about how much agency we want our appliances to have, and how they should balance user preferences with inferred well-being concerns.

Unlike LG agentic countertop EgoLectual™ line of ovens that out right refused to cook something based on such a mysteriously conjured ad-hoc policy, the Breville fulfilled the request — but with a variation, cooking only one slice of bacon of the six in the oven. The result was that the single slice of bacon was fine — and the others were left raw and, obviously, unedible.

Subsequent attempts met with a stern refusal which left only one option: return the raw, greasy bacon to the refrigerator. (And, yes..I tried to coax the stove top to ignore the interlinked MCP attempts to prevent a pan fry of the remaining slices.)

At this point this reviewer was essentially complying as there was no time to continue the negotiations with the commute to work imposing a “hard-out” constraint.

AGENTIC BERRY BOWLS

NEAR FUTURE LABORATORY

This example is the kind of intervention that will divide households quickly. Similar unspecified deviations occured for cookies, brownies, donuts, and mini-cakes. Some people will appreciate the nudge. Others will reasonably feel that one should not have to negotiate with a countertop oven in order to get the breakfast you wanted.

KITCHENAI AGENTIC ESPRESSO EXTRUDER

COUNTERTOP COFFEE SOLUTIONS INC.

The important thing is that the Breville still feels like an oven. It has tactile controls, a restrained interface, and a clear local fallback mode when connectivity drops. That fallback produced more ordinary results, but it was reassuring: the appliance did not become useless just because the orchestration layer stepped back. At 4.2 out of 5, it is the best example here of agentic behavior becoming practical enough to recommend.

Best bedside object: Sony ORACULATOR™ P6502

The Sony ORACULATOR™ P6502 is harder to score because it is less obviously an appliance in the traditional sense. It is an alarm clock, but its real function is daily guidance. Each morning, shortly before the alarm, it prints a thermal-paper emanation: a compact note about likely delays, interpersonal frictions, timing suggestions, and small risks in the day ahead.

The best thing about the Sony is its restraint. There is no chatty assistant voice, no glowing companion, no simulated warmth. It's cool in its emanations, and recites its oraculations as if they were (or are?) matters of fact: the P6502 prints and stops. That single decision makes the product feel less like a chatbot on a nightstand and more like a domestic instrument with a narrowly defined job to do. It is a clock that happens to have a printer, not a printer that happens to be a clock. The result is a product that is easier to admire than to recommend broadly, but it is also the most interesting object we've seen since Sony first introduced its line of oraculators two years ago.

Do you have a colleague or client who would enjoy this? Product fiction like this that translates signals into artifacts can help teams to surface unknowns, provide a surface onto which implications an be assessed and risks can be exposed early. Share this article with them now. It's way better than sharing a PowerPoint or a PDF.

Share This Now

The hardware helps. The compact body, smoked print housing, tactile switches, recessed LEDs, and sunflower-yellow shell give the device the dense authority of older Sony equipment without turning it into nostalgia theater. It looks serious, even when the category sounds faintly absurd. You press the buttons because the buttons seem to matter.

The guidance was occasionally useful. It anticipated delayed transit, suggested leaving earlier before a backed-up errand, and warned one reviewer to avoid an avoidable conversation until later in the day. The problem is that useful guidance from a bedside object has a different emotional texture than useful heat control from an oven. You start noticing how quickly a suggestion can become a plan, and how quickly a plan can feel like your own.

IT MADE ITS OWN BOOZE

BOOZY BITMAPPED BEV BY BUZZ BALLZ

Sony and Anthropic describe the system as probabilistic rather than predictive. That distinction is intellectually useful, but in the morning it does not always feel meaningful. When a small machine gives you a plausible warning before coffee that you will likely lose your job that day — or get into a car accident — the question is not whether it has predicted the future, or is a friendly bit of vague astrological advice. Rather, the question is how much of your day you want to spend ruminating or dealing with its printed-out overconfidence.

Most households should wait to see how this oraculators like this handle dependency, privacy, and the subtle influence of advice that can become addictive — or for which there is no recourse for deeper explanation or reasoning. The Sony ORACULATOR™ is a fascinating object, but it is not for everyone.

Capsule review: Braun Facial Prognosticator

The Braun x Oraculator Prognostic InferenceMate arrived too late for full testing, but its polished hardware made it difficult to ignore.

The Braun Facial Prognosticator arrived too late in our testing cycle for a full evaluation, but after several days with it, we did not want to leave it out entirely. Positioned somewhere between a skincare appliance and a biometric-based prognosticator, the InferenceMate combines facial imaging, behavioral analysis, and anticipatory recommendation apparatus into a surprisingly calm daily-use product.

The product design is excellent. The padded facial cradle is soft and comfortable against the skin, the handle feels balanced and well engineered, and the industrial design is unmistakably Braun: restrained, ergonomic, and carefully resolved. The prognostic interface is understated, surfacing small daily recommendations for behavior adjustments, offering social advisories for complicated anticipated interactions with friends and colleagues — even relationship advice, astrological pattern matrices and your daily anticipatory indices presented in a clean monochrome display that feels less like the mystical “woo-woo” of a horoscope and more like the kind of data-driven insights that could be useful particularly when they are presented in a way that feels more like a personal coach than a fortune teller.

The cognitive catastrophe?

An oven that can decide that your stated preference conflicts with its model of a better outcome? A clock that may make it easy to treat it as wiser than it deserves to be? Neither behavior is catastrophic — but both are subtle and potential pernicious enough to result in a kind of new normal before anyone notices that a new, somewhat problematic standard is being set by a couple of consumer appliances.

But, some will say — so did the television remote control, which kept us from getting up to change the channel. Now, with an oraculating alarm clock, we may have our days pre-determined based on inference and prediction from a machine that we don't fully understand. The difference is that the remote control was a tool for executing our decisions — our judgment — while these appliances are making decisions on our behalf, which can lead to a loss of agency and autonomy over time if not designed with care.

Explainer

This is a speculative product review artifact from the Near Future Laboratory's anticipatory research platform “The Adjacency”. I do these kinds of things to explore possible futures of technology and society in a way that is more expansive than a report or a flat, text-heavy trend analysis. It's way more generative than a PowerPoint deck. If your organization is interested in commissioning this kind of work to communicate a roadmap, test a product category, or make strategic possibilities easier to examine, get in touch.

Editorial Remarks

These speculative artifacts imagine-into a possible future of agentic appliances — what we used to call “smart appliances.” The products reviewed are fictional — just in case you're wondering — but this is important: they are grounded in current trends and technologies in the consumer appliance industry. By using speculative fictional contrivances, this kind of research gets to explore the potential benefits and challenges of introducing agentic reasoning into household appliances, treating it as a feature that can enhance utility when designed with clear boundaries, legibility, and user control. The review also addresses concerns about privacy, agency, and the balance between user preferences and inferred well-being. The intent is to provoke thought about how these kinds of products might fit into everyday life and what trade-offs they might entail.

The research “grounding” behind this may feel intuitive if you've been steeped in this world of LLMs and AI and all the rest or, like me, you are a researcher, a product designer, and basically an inhabitant of the liminal future for some time.

In any case, it is important to have some strong ties to extant research, news, trend analysis, so that the speculative work is not seen as just unmoored fantasy or “pure” science-fiction (whatever that might mean.)

This is the grounding section. Think of it either as the references referred to, or as waypoints to the same story as above, but told in a different idiolect.

Enjoy. And please support this work over on Patreon or get in touch and commission this kind of work for your organization.

Referenced Signals

[1]Kitchen Cosmo: The AI Appliance That Turns Leftovers into Recipes

An MIT AI kitchen appliance that turns leftovers into recipes.

[2]A smart home is one that talks to itself

Smart-home devices communicating with each other through context-aware, multimodal, and animistic design — a ubicomp and household intelligence frame.

[3]Going down the Nabaztag rabbit hole

The Nabaztag was an early internet-connected device (still ahead of its time) that could perform various functions like reading emails, weather updates, and even dancing. It was a speculative prototype to modern smart home devices and showcased the potential of connected appliances in a domestic setting in a way that wasn't overly extractive — but grounded in mechatronic fun and whimsy.

[4]Berg's Little Printer: A Charming Blend of Nostalgia and Connectivity

The Little Printer was a small, internet-connected device that printed out news, weather, and personal messages on receipt paper. It was designed to bring a sense of nostalgia and physicality to digital information, demonstrating how connected appliances can create unique user experiences in the home. Proto-animistic and domestic quirkiness. Hi. Timo? Jack? You there? 📲

[5]Amazon Horrified by What People Actually Use Alexa For

Amazon's Alexa is being used mostly for banal tasks like timers and alarms — might it come to pass that agentic appliances must stay useful as appliances first without the sci-fi household assumptions that designers and marketers assume will be their primary use cases. It makes me wonder how much of the appeal of agentic appliances is still living in a science-fictional universe when people just want the same things as before — convenience and reliability, and introducing a new kind of alien reasoning into the mix may result in more confusion, breakdowns, and such.

[6]The House That Spied on Me

A connected-home privacy experiment, grounding the concern that household appliances can expose routines, preferences, and intimate domestic patterns. The next privacy frontier is not just data collection, but the inferences and influence that can come from appliances that know too much about the household.

[7]How Americans Feel About AI's ImpactHow Americans View Ai And Its Impact On People And Society

Pew Center reports about public concern over AI's influence, desire for personal control, and preservation of human abilities, and how AI experts vs. the general US public view AI. These address and ground notions of agency and autonomy and associated concerns.

[8]The Future is Mundane

Rather than focusing solely on grand trends or technological leaps, Sarah Pink urges us to pay attention to the lived, sensory realities of daily life when thinking about the future. She explains how anthropology, once focused only on the past and present, is now increasingly interested in what everyday life will feel like years from now, especially as climate change and new technologies reshape our routines. By foregrounding the human experience—how we want to feel, live, and interact—Pink believes we can imagine more meaningful, grounded futures. Her work bridges anthropology and design, emphasizing that uncertainty isn't just a challenge but a space for exploring new possibilities.

[9]Moltbot Points to the Future of Personal AI Assistants

Moltbot, which was known as Clawdbot until a recent name change, is an advanced personal AI assistant running on Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.5 model. It remembers personal details like your name and daily preferences, seamlessly integrates with productivity tools like Notion and Todoist, and can control devices like Spotify, Sonos speakers, Philips Hue lights, and even Gmail. The assistant operates through Telegram, making it easy to interact with, including through voice messages. The author named their assistant Navi, and after spending a week using it, was impressed by how personalized and integrated the experience felt compared to traditional digital assistants. Moltbot offers a glimpse of how AI companions could soon become truly personal, proactive, and seamlessly embedded in our digital lives.

[10]Talkie Toaster

Talkie Toaster is a minor character in the British science fiction comedy series 'Red Dwarf.' It is a sentient toaster that is obsessed with making toast and often engages in humorous conversations with the crew of the spaceship Red Dwarf. The Talkie Toaster is known for its catchphrase, 'Toast! Toast! Toast!' and its relentless pursuit of perfect toast, which often leads to comedic situations. The character serves as a lighthearted exploration of artificial intelligence and its potential quirks when applied to everyday appliances.

[11]Agentic toaster and smart appliance failure

A signal-only grounding reference for agentic toaster behavior, smart appliance failure, and domestic resilience when everyday machines become conversational, needy, or unreliable.
